For $x\notin P$, choose an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $E\cap U$ is at most countable. Thus $P^c$ is open, so $P$ is closed.

We claim that $P$ has no isolated points. Let $x\in P$ and let $r>0$. Assume that $B(x,r)\cap P=\{x\}$. For each $y\in B(x,r)\setminus\{x\}$, since $y\notin P$, choose an open neighborhood $U_y$ such that $E\cap U_y$ is at most countable. By second countability of $\mathbb R^k$, the cover of $B(x,r)\setminus\{x\}$ by the sets $U_y$ has a countable subcover $U_{y_1},U_{y_2},\ldots$. Therefore
\[
E\cap(B(x,r)\setminus\{x\})\subseteq\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}(E\cap U_{y_n}),
\]
which is at most countable. Adding $x$ preserves countability, so $E\cap B(x,r)$ is at most countable, contradicting $x\in P$.

Thus every point of $P$ is a limit point of $P$. Since $P$ is closed, it is perfect.
\end{proof}

\[
E\cap(B(x,r)\setminus\{x\})

\]

Therefore $P$ is closed and has no isolated points. Consequently, $P$ is perfect.
